rationale: Start with a broad mid-length scouting gradient spanning almost the full solvent-strength range at a moderate temperature to reveal overall retention spread, missing late eluters, and clustering. This gives a balanced first map of the 10-component mixture without being excessively slow.

All 10 compounds eluted with excellent resolution and substantial unused time, so the fastest path to a higher CRF is to shorten the gradient while keeping composition and temperature fixed. A 10 min gradient should compress the run and test how much time can be saved before the closest mid-run cluster loses critical resolution.

The fast method compressed a central cluster too much, especially peaks 5–7, so the next move is to make the gradient shallower while keeping the same run length and temperature. Lowering phi1 should reduce gradient steepness across the region where all compounds already elute and may spread that mid-run group without sacrificing the already excellent time term.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.80 improved the critical 6/7 separation while keeping the run short, so continue that trend with a slightly shallower 10 min gradient. This should further spread the tightly packed mid-eluting cluster and may push the resolution term closer to 1.0 without introducing a time penalty.

The same trend continues: progressively shallower gradients are specifically improving the persistent 6/7 critical pair while all compounds still elute quickly. Dropping phi1 one more step should test whether that pair can be pushed above 1.5 and potentially maximize the resolution term while likely retaining zero time penalty.

At phi1 0.60 the resolution term reached 1.000 but incurred a modest time penalty, so the optimum is likely between 0.60 and 0.70. Testing the midpoint should preserve full resolution while shortening the run enough to beat the current best CRF.

The current best is very close to ideal, with only the 6/7 pair slightly below 1.5, so a small increase in gradient time is the least disruptive way to gain a bit more resolution. Keeping phi0 and phi1 fixed while extending tG from 10 to 12 min should selectively relax that crowded region with only a minimal risk of a time penalty.

The best method is already near-optimal, and changing tG upward cost too much time, so the next fine-tuning lever is temperature. A modest drop to 35 C may slightly improve selectivity in the critical 6/7 region while keeping retention increase smaller than the tG change did.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so probe the opposite direction with a small increase to 45 C while holding the otherwise best conditions. This is the cleanest remaining local test to see whether the critical mid-cluster separation improves above the 40 C result without adding time.

Keep the best phi1, tG, and temperature, but raise phi0 by one grid step to reduce the overall gradient span from 0.60 to 0.55. This is a small, targeted selectivity test that may relieve the central crowding without the larger time cost seen when extending tG.

You already reached the maximum CRF, so any further run is exploratory only. This nearby variant tests whether a slightly shallower gradient preserves full resolution and zero time penalty, helping confirm how broad the optimum is around the winning method.

Since the optimum has already been found, the useful remaining question is how sharply tuned it is. Testing the symmetric neighbor on the stronger-gradient side maps robustness around the winning method and checks whether CRF stays near-maximal when phi1 is increased one step.

The winning point suggests phi1 = 0.65 is ideal while slightly higher phi0 improved the critical pair versus the 0.05 start, so testing phi0 one more step higher maps whether that benefit continues. This is a close local probe around the optimum and could reveal whether the maximum is broad or sharply centered at phi0 = 0.10.

You now have two adjacent phi0 values giving the maximum CRF, so the next informative step is to test whether the 1.000 plateau extends further upward. This nearby condition maps robustness of the optimum and checks whether additional increase in phi0 begins to compress the early region too much.

With a maximum-CRF method already found, the remaining worthwhile test is whether the same selectivity window can be made even faster while staying on the 1.000 plateau. The best region is clearly around phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.65, and lowering phi1 at phi0 0.10 only cost a small time penalty while keeping full resolution. Testing the analogous point at phi0 0.15 explores whether that higher start can offset the time cost and reveal another robust maximum neighborhood.

You have now bracketed the optimum on the lower-phi1 side at phi0 0.15, so the symmetric higher-phi1 neighbor is the natural final local check in this robust maximum region. This maps the shape of the 1.000 plateau around the second optimum without moving away from the clearly favorable conditions.

The optimum is already secured, so remaining runs can characterize robustness rather than improve score. A larger temperature drop at the winning composition maps thermal sensitivity more completely than the earlier ±5 C tests and may reveal whether selectivity changes systematically across the critical cluster.

The large temperature decrease caused major selectivity changes, so the complementary high-temperature extreme is the most informative remaining robustness check at the winning composition. This will complete the thermal map and show whether the optimum is centered near 40 C or bordered by another selectivity regime.

The temperature extremes revealed strong selectivity changes at the 0.10/0.65 optimum, so testing the second 1.000 method at low temperature will show whether the higher starting strength is more thermally robust. This is the most informative remaining comparison within the already proven optimal family.

The low-temperature test on the second optimal method also showed severe selectivity distortion, so the complementary high-temperature extreme completes the robustness comparison for that optimal family. This will show whether both 1.000 methods share the same thermal sensitivity pattern or diverge at elevated temperature.

Two exact-optimum methods have been found, and the surrounding map suggests the plateau likely ends as phi0 increases further. Testing phi0 0.25 at the otherwise favorable settings defines that upper boundary and checks whether early-elution compression becomes limiting.

With only two runs left and the optimum already secured, the most informative remaining comparison is the short-gradient counterpart of the original phi0 0.05 series to complete the local map of speed versus resolution. This helps separate whether the improvement at higher phi0 came mainly from starting strength or from avoiding overcompression at shorter effective gradients.

For the final run, test a nearby untried point that balances the upper-phi0 limit found at 0.25/0.65 and the lower-phi1 full-resolution behavior seen at 0.15/0.60.
